subject: Business
title: Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
description: A short lesson to help you apply Decision-Making Under Uncertainty.

hook.text: Jeff Bezos says most decisions should be made with about 70% of the information. Wait for 90% and you're too slow.

buildup.text: Uncertainty is the default state for leaders. Perfect information never arrives in time.

discovery.text: Bezos distinguishes 'one-way doors' (irreversible) from 'two-way doors' (reversible). Only the first need caution.

twist.text: Analysis paralysis costs more than wrong decisions. A good decision made quickly beats a perfect decision made late.

climax.text: Amazon's bias for action over perfection drove its expansion from books to everything.

punchline.text: Decide fast on reversible choices. Decide carefully on permanent ones.

quiz.question: What is Bezos's framework for decision speed?
options: Decide fast on reversible 'two-way door' decisions; be careful with irreversible 'one-way doors'
Always wait for 100% of the information
Delegate all decisions to avoid personal risk

details.summary: Leaders must make consequential decisions with incomplete information, balancing the cost of waiting for more data against the cost of acting too soon. Effective approaches include setting decision deadlines, using reversible decisions, and applying probabilistic thinking to uncertain outcomes.
details.whyItMatters: In a fast-moving business environment, waiting for perfect information means deciding too late. Leaders who can make sound decisions with 70 percent of the information available outperform those who delay seeking 95 percent certainty.
takeaways: Waiting for perfect information often means deciding too late to matter
Classify decisions as reversible or irreversible to calibrate required certainty
Jeff Bezos advocates deciding at 70 percent information for reversible decisions

faq.question: How do you distinguish between decisions that need more analysis and those where speed matters most?
faq.answer: Irreversible, high-stakes decisions warrant more analysis and deliberation. Reversible, lower-stakes decisions should be made quickly and corrected if wrong. Most decisions are reversible but leaders treat them as permanent, creating unnecessary bottlenecks and analysis paralysis.

faq.question: What frameworks help leaders make decisions with incomplete information?
faq.answer: Pre-mortem analysis imagines failure before deciding. Expected value calculations weight outcomes by probability. Decision journals track reasoning for later review. Time-boxing prevents analysis paralysis by forcing decisions within deadlines. Scenario planning prepares multiple responses.
